name: Workflow orchestration
summary: A durable state machine that drives multi-step processes to completion.
howItWorks: You define the steps of a process, their order, and what happens on failure: retries with backoff, timeouts, branches, parallel steps and compensating actions. The engine records every transition, so a process can wait days for a person or an outside system and resume exactly where it left off, even after a crash.
analogy: A project manager with a checklist who never forgets where each project stands, chases late steps, and follows the backup plan when something fails.
useWhen: Processes that span services: order fulfilment, onboarding, data pipelines
Long waits on people, approvals or callbacks
Replacing tangled chains of queues and cron jobs that nobody can debug
avoidWhen: One quick step; a function or queue is enough
example: An order workflow validates the cart, tries to charge the card up to 3 times, then ships. If the charge is declined, it runs a compensation step that releases the reserved stock and tells the customer.

story: Business processes have always spanned many steps and long stretches of time: an order is checked, paid for, packed and shipped; an insurance claim moves from desk to desk. In 1987 Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem of Princeton described “sagas”: a long-lived transaction written as a sequence of smaller ones, with compensating transactions to undo a partial run. Their examples were monthly bank statements and insurance claims.

The 1990s brought workflow management systems, and the Workflow Management Coalition, founded in 1993, worked to standardize them. IBM and Microsoft merged their web-service orchestration languages, WSFL and XLANG, into BPEL4WS, an XML language that they, BEA, SAP and Siebel submitted to the OASIS standards body in 2003. Cloud providers and web companies then brought the idea to developers: Amazon’s Simple Workflow Service in 2012, Airbnb’s Apache Airflow for data pipelines in 2015, AWS Step Functions in 2016, and Uber’s Cadence, which became Temporal, where workflows are ordinary code.

Today the idea often goes by “durable execution”: the engine records every step, so a process can wait days for a person or survive a crash and resume where it stopped. AI agents, which run long chains of model and tool calls, have renewed interest; Temporal raised $550 million in 2026 as demand grew for reliable AI infrastructure.

choices.choice: One engine owns the whole process
choices.why: A central orchestrator knows every step and where each instance stands, so failures, timeouts and stuck steps show up in one place instead of being scattered across queues and cron jobs.
Holding database locks for a process that runs hours or days blocks everything else, so sagas commit each step and undo completed ones with compensating actions if a later step fails.
Writing each step down durably lets the engine resume after a crash, and lets a process sleep for days without holding a server.

choices.choice: Definitions as data, or workflows as code
choices.why: BPEL and Step Functions describe the process as XML or JSON that an engine can validate and draw. Cadence and Temporal use a normal programming language instead, which requires deterministic code so the engine can replay it.

BPEL4WS, from IBM and Microsoft, is submitted to OASIS
